questions.question_text:
A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.25(M-40)$.
What does the number $40$ represent in this model?

options.text: The fixed value that $M$ approaches if initially different from it, and remains at if initially equal to it.

options.why: Confuses the fixed value $P$ with the starting value $M(0)$, which the equation does not give.

options.text: The rate of change of $M$ at $t=0$.
options.why: Reads a constant inside the bracket as a rate; the rate is $-0.25(M-40)$.

options.text: The fixed value that $M$ moves away from.
options.why: Ignores the sign of $k$; with $k=-0.25<0$, $M$ approaches $40$ if initially different from it, and remains at $40$ if initially equal to it.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=k(M-P)$ with $k=-0.25$ and $P=40$
Since $k<0$, the magnitude of the gap $|M-40|$ shrinks when it is nonzero, so $M$ approaches the fixed value $40$ if initially different from it.
If $M$ is initially $40$, the rate is zero and $M$ remains at $40$.

questions.question_text:
A pie at $150^{\circ}$C is placed in a fridge kept at $4^{\circ}$C. The pie cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature $T$ and the fridge temperature.
Using the convention $k<0$, which differential equation models this?

options.why: Uses the pie's starting temperature as the fixed value instead of the fridge temperature.
Reverses the difference; with the specified $k<0$ and $T>4$, this gives a positive rate and warming.
Both errors together: the starting temperature is used as the fixed value and the difference is reversed.

questions.solution_text:
The fixed value is the temperature of the surroundings, so $P=4$.
$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-4)$, where $k<0$.

questions.question_text:
A tray of ice cream at $-16^{\circ}$C is left on a bench in a room at $23^{\circ}$C, and warms according to $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-23)$.
Which statement about $k$ is correct?

options.text: $k<0$, because the gap $T-23$ is negative while the temperature is rising.
$k>0$, because the temperature of the ice cream is increasing.
options.why: Matches the sign of $k$ to the sign of $\frac{dT}{dt}$ without allowing for the negative difference $T-23$.

options.text: $k>0$, because the ice cream is colder than the room.
options.why: Treats the positive temperature shortfall $23-T$ as the bracket in the given equation, instead of the negative difference $T-23$.

options.text: $k<0$, because the ice cream is losing energy to the room.
options.why: Reaches the right sign from a false physical claim: the ice cream gains energy from the warmer room.

questions.solution_text:
While the ice cream is colder than the room, $T-23<0$.
The ice cream is warming, so $\dfrac{dT}{dt}>0$.
A negative difference times $k$ is positive only when $k<0$.

questions.question_text:
An object initially at $90^{\circ}$C cools according to $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.04(T-25)$.
What is its limiting temperature?

options.why: Uses the initial temperature instead of the fixed value approached as time increases.
Uses the initial difference $90-25=65$ instead of the limiting temperature.
Assumes cooling approaches zero, ignoring the fixed temperature $25$ in the bracket.

questions.solution_text:
Here $k=-0.04<0$, so the temperature approaches the fixed value $25$.
The limiting temperature is $25^{\circ}$C.

questions.question_text:
A tub of yoghurt at $5^{\circ}$C is left in a room at $27^{\circ}$C, and its temperature obeys $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-P)$.
What are the values of $P$ and of the initial difference $T(0)-P$?

options.why: Takes the size of the gap without its sign; the yoghurt starts below room temperature.
Uses the yoghurt's starting temperature as the fixed value and the room temperature as the starting value.
Incorrectly sets $P$ to the initial temperature while separately retaining the actual initial-minus-room difference $5-27=-22$.

questions.solution_text:
The surroundings give the fixed value, so $P=27$.
$T(0)-P=5-27$
$=-22$

questions.question_text:
A lake supports at most $2000$ fish, and the population $N$ obeys $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k(N-2000)$.
When there are $500$ fish the population is growing at $45$ fish per week.
What is the value of $k$?

options.why: Divides by $2000-500$ instead of $500-2000$, losing the negative sign that growth towards the capacity requires.
Divides the rate by the population $500$ rather than by the difference $500-2000$.
Uses the negative capacity $-2000$ as the denominator instead of the difference $500-2000$, giving $45/(-2000)=-0.0225$.

questions.question_text:
A casserole initially at $96^{\circ}$C cools in a room at $18^{\circ}$C according to $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-18)$ with $k<0$.
What is the limiting temperature of the casserole?

options.why: Confuses the initial temperature with the limiting temperature.
Uses the initial temperature difference $96-18=78$ as the limiting temperature.
Assumes a negative constant makes the temperature approach zero, ignoring the fixed value $18$.

questions.solution_text:
Since $k<0$, the magnitude of the gap $|T-18|$ shrinks and $T\rightarrow18$ as $t\rightarrow\infty$.
The limiting temperature is $18^{\circ}$C.

questions.question_text:
A body cools in air kept at $18^{\circ}$C, following $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-18)$.
At the instant its temperature is $78^{\circ}$C it is cooling at $4.2^{\circ}$C per minute.
What is the value of $k$?

options.why: Uses the positive cooling-rate magnitude $4.2$ as the signed derivative, giving $4.2/60=0.07$.
Makes a decimal-place error when dividing $-4.2$ by $78-18=60$.
Uses the signed temperature rate directly as $k$ without dividing by the temperature difference $60$.
